articles.title: Utilizing digital ethnography techniques to expand walkthrough method using participant-generated media
articles.abstract: Walkthrough has found modern application as a methodology in user experience scholarship and practice to allow researchers to qualitatively “walk,” step-by-step, through a digital interface and examine functions, communication, implications, and usability. Simultaneously, existing users of digital platforms have begun creating media of themselves walking through properties for the benefit of their digital communities, leading to the rise of user-generated walkthroughs. These user-generated walkthroughs share user experience, provide situated expertise, and circulate knowledge within digital communities. Despite this growth, walkthrough methodology has largely developed within UX and human–computer interaction contexts and lacks deeper integration with social scientific and ethnographic priorities. User-generated walkthroughs in communication research present a unique opportunity to bridge these traditions by bringing the rigor and epistemological commitments of digital ethnography into conversation with walkthrough practice. In doing so, participant-generated walkthroughs center participant knowledge, positioning users as active interpreters who signal what is meaningful in digital environments. This manuscript proposes theoretical and methodological directions for future participant-generated walkthrough research, arguing that digital ethnographic considerations provide the necessary structure for more rigorous and socially grounded applications of the Walkthrough method, while also opening new possibilities for qualitative and computational inquiry in digital spaces.

articles.title: Global reach, local constraints: senior professionals on the streamers’ impact on creative power, autonomy, and authorship in the Flemish audiovisual industry
articles.abstract: Streaming platforms have transformed opportunities for European filmmakers, providing global reach and essential additional funding. However, these platforms also challenge notions of creative autonomy and authorship. Insights derived from thirteen in-depth interviews with senior industry professionals from the Flemish film and audiovisual market – primarily filmmakers, producers, and other professional stakeholders – reveal the complexities of this evolving creative landscape. This offers deeper insights into the interrelated challenges of creative freedom and collaboration with streamers. Three key perspectives emerge. First, almost all interviewed professionals acknowledge streaming platforms’ importance regarding additional financing. Over the last decade, these have increasingly become important as additional investors in an ecosystem increasingly challenged by a strained economic environment. Second, stakeholders highlight concerns over creative control when working with streamers. Although these platforms offer vital resources, they often impose rigid guidelines to cater to algorithm-driven global audiences, limiting filmmakers’ autonomy and control over final cuts. The third perspective suggests a convergence of cinema, streaming formats, and creative practices. Many directors are drawn to the series format for its potential for extended storytelling and its capability to sustain audiences’ attention for longer periods. This interplay creates new creative opportunities but also blurs the lines between traditional cinematic and serialized narratives and content, while simultaneously fostering homogenization processes.

articles.title: Expanded documentary and immersive technologies: Ludic logics and heritage mediation in ARTE’s interactive experiences
articles.abstract: This article examines the transformation of contemporary documentary practices through immersive and interactive technologies, including virtual reality, augmented reality and game-based narrative structures. Positioned within debates on media convergence, the study argues that expanded documentary forms do not merely hybridise non-fiction with entertainment but reconfigure documentary epistemology through embodied immersion, procedural authorship and guided participation. Drawing on theories of expanded cinema, interactive documentary and game studies, the article clarifies the concept of ludic logics and distinguishes it from gamification and serious games. A qualitative comparative analysis of emblematic immersive documentary projects is conducted using a shared analytical grid focused on immersion, agency, narrative organisation and ethical positioning. The findings show that immersive non-fiction fosters situated and affective forms of knowledge while introducing new tensions between agency and authorial control. The article contributes to documentary and media convergence studies by providing a conceptually precise and methodologically replicable framework for analysing immersive non-fiction.

articles.title: Platformed nostalgia: Techlash and the commercialisation of historical social media nostalgia on Tumblr
articles.abstract: This article conceptualises platformed nostalgia as a social media platform branding strategy that commodifies historical social media nostalgia to (re)gain social acceptance and legitimacy in response to popular techlash towards contemporary social media platforms. Drawing on a critical discourse analysis of 193 marketing and platform communication documents authored by and/or related to Tumblr under Automattic’s ownership (2019-), it argues that platformed nostalgia is cultivated through platform branding and communication strategies that instrumentalise users’ assumed nostalgic attachments to an imagined utopic past of early social media alongside normative platform values of transparency, democracy, and public good. The findings reveal that, in Tumblr’s case, the latter are invoked to position the platform as a nostalgic foil to real or imagined irresponsible or less responsible corporate social media platforms of the present, such as X (formerly Twitter). The analysis therefore explores how popular forms of historical social media nostalgia emerging from discontentment with and critique of the technocultural present are vulnerable to commercial co-optation by social media platforms.

articles.title: Finding Love in the Black Box: Algorithm Awareness on Dating Apps
articles.authors: Doris Bukman, Liesel L. Sharabi, Elisabeth Timmermans
articles.abstract: Most dating apps use algorithms to match users to one another, but are not fully transparent about how their recommender systems work. In turn, users have varying degrees of awareness of matching algorithms. Unfortunately, little is known about how awareness of algorithmic functioning relates to online dating. This research examined the relationship between algorithm awareness, trust in algorithms, and satisfaction with the quality of matches. A survey was conducted among 500 users of the Dutch dating app Breeze, presented to respondents within the app itself. Relationships were estimated with structural equation modeling. Higher algorithm awareness was associated with more trust in algorithms, which positively related to satisfaction with the quality of matches. This mediated association between awareness and satisfaction with matches suggested that awareness of matching algorithms is associated with better outcomes of dating app use. This research contributes to the limited literature on human–algorithm interaction on dating apps. Overall, the results suggest that algorithm awareness may be a relevant part of the online dating experience.

Keeping Ms. Pac-Man Out of the Club: Pacmania, Video Game Magazines, and the Gendered Guardrails of Digital Worlds in the Early 1980s
articles.abstract: This article reveals a gendered backlash to the increased participation of female gamers during Pacmania in the United States in the early 1980s. As Pac-Man and Ms. Pac-Man gained immense national recognition, gaming magazines, newsletters, and newspaper articles recognized the female gamers who contributed to tournaments and gaming culture. However, some male gamers mocked “cute” games, coded to female gamers, that supposedly undermined the stature attached to “serious” games. Present throughout gaming media but epitomized in the gaming magazine VIDIOT , this set of male gamers mocked female gamers and cute games that somehow undeservedly encroached upon their digital domain. This antiPacmania backlash was an early historical moment in which male gamers and corporate institutions installed gendered guardrails to preserve video games as an exclusive realm that marginalized females. This moment was an early case study of the gendered ideals that shaped the next decades’ male-focused advertising and even Gamergate.

articles.title: Replenishing resources with enterprise social media (ESM): overload-moderated effects on work-life balance, exhaustion, and turnover
articles.authors: Murad Moqbel, Mohamed Hédi Charki, Amr Soror
articles.abstract: Purpose This study investigates the double-edged impact of Enterprise social media (ESM) use on employee well-being through Conservation of Resources (COR) theory. We examine how work- and nonwork-related ESM use affects work exhaustion and turnover intention via work–life balance (WLB), and how these effects are contingent on perceived work overload. Design/methodology/approach A survey was administered to professionals at a major IT corporation in the Midwestern United States. Data from 276 employees were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Findings Only nonwork-related ESM use directly promotes WLB. Both work-related and nonwork-related ESM use enhances WLB for employees experiencing high perceived work overload. WLB negatively affects work exhaustion and turnover intention, and work exhaustion positively predicts turnover intention. Perceived work overload is a critical boundary condition shaping the impact of ESM use. Research limitations/implications Because this sample was drawn from a single organization, future research should extend these findings longitudinally and test other ESM-driven spillovers, such as effects on family life. Managers should replace blanket ESM policies with workload-differentiated strategies, encouraging ESM use as a coping resource under high demand while fostering psychologically safe connectivity norms. Originality/value The study offers a contingency-based perspective that reconciles apparent contradictions in ESM literature, moving beyond asking whether ESM has an impact to explaining how and when its effects manifest. A key theoretical contribution is the identification of perceived work overload as a factor that can transform ESM use from a potential drain on resources into a vital coping tool for employee well-being.

articles.title: More, shorter, newer? How monetization reshapes creator strategy on YouTube Shorts
articles.authors: Soonjae Kwon, Kitae Kim, Sung-Hyuk Park
articles.abstract: Purpose This study examines the causal impact of YouTube Shorts' ad-revenue sharing policy on creator production strategies in the short-form video creator economy. Design/methodology/approach Using 36,507 videos from 342 top global channels, we employ a regression discontinuity in time design. Computer vision techniques measure four attributes of each creator's production strategy: output volume, video length, editing pace, and content novelty. Findings The policy drove an immediate reduction in video length without expanding output volume, consistent with substitution toward cheaper per-unit configurations rather than output scaling. Entertainment creators shortened their videos most sharply, while informative creators slowed their editing pace to preserve comprehension. Long-type creators pursued per-unit cost reduction, while short-type creators invested in content novelty. Research limitations/implications The sample covers top-tier global channels, so emerging creators may respond differently. The findings show that the quantity-expansion result from low-marginal-cost user-generated content settings does not extend to high-marginal-cost production, where incentives reallocate effort within existing output rather than expand it. Practical implications A uniform monetization policy does not produce uniform outcomes. Incentive design should anticipate that creators adjust different production attributes depending on their content goals and capabilities. Originality/value This study provides causal evidence that performance-contingent monetization reshapes production strategy in a high-cost video production context and that one platform-wide policy generates different responses across creator types.

articles.title: IT professionals' alumni networks and firm innovation: the role of informal connections in dynamic environments
articles.authors: Binger Lin, Chunmian Ge, Junhui Jiang, Yichao Xu
articles.abstract: Purpose We aim to address a critical organizational challenge – how firms can leverage informal networks to enhance innovation in increasingly dynamic environments. Alumni networks connect IT professionals and support knowledge exchange across geographical and organizational boundaries, facilitating innovation through distributed collaboration. However, prior studies have inadequately examined whether and how alumni networks help IT professionals overcome boundary barriers and contribute to firm innovation. Our study fills this gap and offers practical implications for management policies. Design/methodology/approach Using data from a large online professional social networking platform, we construct alumni networks of IT professionals and use linear regression and Poisson models to examine their impact on firm innovation. This study also conducts several robustness tests, including reconstructing the alumni networks, adopting alternative centrality measures, applying different thresholds to identify high-centrality IT professionals and using lagged independent variables. Findings We find that firms with more IT professionals occupying central positions in the alumni network exhibit stronger innovation performance. Furthermore, this positive relationship is strengthened in conditions of high technological and market dynamism, highlighting the value of informal networks in driving innovation in dynamic environments. Originality/value The positive effect of IT professionals' alumni networks on firm innovation extends the understanding of informal networks by highlighting their significance in facilitating information access and integration across organizational boundaries. We further illustrate how the impact of alumni networks varies with environmental dynamism, offering practical insights into how firms can strengthen resilience and adaptive capacity in response to environmental uncertainty.

articles.title: Measuring consumer literacy about online fraud: effects on perceived financial risk and trust in online sellers
articles.abstract: Purpose This study aims to develop and validate a scale to measure consumer literacy about online fraud (CLOF). While prior research has linked general education and financial literacy to fraud victimization, specific knowledge about online fraud remains underexplored. The CLOF scale addresses this gap by capturing consumers' awareness of fraud-related practices and protective behaviors. The study also examines the relationships between CLOF and perceived financial risk, trust in online sellers, and online buying intensity. Design/methodology/approach Following established scale development procedures, we conducted focus groups, item generation, Q-sort validation, and pilot testing. The CLOF scale was tested across three studies in the USA, Sweden, and the UK using exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses. Reliability and validity were assessed through Cronbach's alpha, composite reliability, AVE, and discriminant validity. Structural equation modeling (SEM) was used to test the hypotheses. Findings The CLOF scale comprises six dimensions (i.e. Knowledge about identity theft; Verification of the legitimacy of companies; Knowledge of how to report fraud; Checking red flags that prevent being a victim of online scams; Knowledge and use of tools that protect against scams; and Reading terms and conditions as a protection practice). The results also show that CLOF is negatively associated with perceived financial risk and positively associated with trust in online sellers. Originality/value Existing scales do not capture literacy about online fraud effectively, with inconsistent literacy–fraud relationships reported in the literature. Hence, there is an urgent need for effective measurement and associated behavior in this context. This research introduces the first validated scale specifically designed to measure consumer literacy about online fraud. The scale offers practical utility for scholars, policymakers, and practitioners aiming to enhance fraud prevention and consumer confidence in e-commerce.

articles.title: Inoculating against fatalistic beliefs: a comparative test of narrative and non-narrative strategies
articles.abstract: This study compares the effectiveness of narrative and non-narrative inoculation messages in reducing fatalistic beliefs and fostering resistance to conflicting cancer information. A two-phase randomized experiment (N = 572 in Phase 1; n = 332 in Phase 2) tested their effects on counterarguing against attack, cancer fatalism, perceived efficacy, and intentions to adopt cancer risk-reduction behaviors. Compared with control, both inoculation messages reduced cancer fatalism, enhanced perceived efficacy, and increased certain intentions to adopt certain risk-reduction behaviors. Narrative inoculation elicited more counterarguing against attack than the non-narrative counterpart. Inoculation effects also varied by baseline fatalism, functioning therapeutically by immediately reducing initially high fatalism and, more modestly, prophylactically by maintaining initially low fatalism. These findings extend inoculation theory by elucidating the role of message format in sustaining resistance to negative media effects, and by demonstrating the theory’s potential dual prophylactic–therapeutic functionality in a fatalistic belief context.

articles.title: It Must Have Been Love (But It's Over Now): Thematic Changes in Popular U.S. Song Lyrics Across 4+ Decades
articles.authors: Janet B. Ruscher, Katherine B. Carnelley
articles.abstract: Over time, U.S. marriage rates have decreased, as people increasingly expect romantic relationships to satisfy high-level needs. Concurrently, interest in sexualized relationships (e.g., hook-ups; consensual nonmonogamy) has increased. Reflecting these patterns over time, song lyrics may become less about prototypical romantic love and more about noncommitted sexual relationships. Using the Meaning Extraction module in LIWC-22, four independent content themes were pulled from the top 25 songs of the Billboard Hot 100 from 1980 to 2024 ( N = 1,129). Themes were correlated with chart year and LIWC linguistic categories. Lyrics high on a Fall in (or out of) Love theme (content words like love, heart, break ) became less common and used past and future tense. In contrast, lyrics high on a Contact theme (e.g., talk, stop, call) became more common, more sexualized (sexual and swear words), and avoided future tense. The advantage of Meaning Extraction for testing hypotheses about language with large data is discussed.

articles.title: How Artificial Intelligence Shapes Human Narratives
articles.abstract: How can artificial intelligence (AI) best support human problem-solving, creativity, and group work? I introduce a psychological account of narrative agency that formalizes how human groups learn from, communicate, and influence narratives in digital contexts. I then discuss how AI models impact human performance through a narrative agency lens, from authoring better essays to finding consensus online. Crucially, AI outputs are routed through a human's narrative agency to generate a result that causes change in the world. Designing human–AI systems around maintaining people's narrative agency is therefore essential for human–AI alignment.

articles.title: African Community Media, AI, and the Question of Community Participation in the Disruptive Era
articles.authors: Lyton Ncube, Allen Munoriyarwa, Albert Chibuwe, Refilwe Whitney Mofokeng, Antonette Kakujaha-Murangi
articles.abstract: In this article, we examine the nexus of Southern African community newspapers’ sceptical AI integration and grassroots democracy. The sceptical approach to AI integration in marginalised media markets of Southern African community newspapers’ news ecosystems is interrogated. We respond to the questions: In what ways is the integration of AI tools in everyday news production routines within Southern African community media institutions defined by scepticism? What is the basis of scepticism amongst Southern African community media journalists? What are the implications for grassroots democracy in these communities? The Southern African community media under study are drawn from South Africa, Zimbabwe, and Namibia. Data were collected through in-depth semi-structured interviews with purposively sampled journalists and editors from these newsrooms. Findings show that the sceptical approach to AI adoption among Southern African community newspapers is largely driven by fears and concerns about AI’s documented mass production of misinformation and disinformation. In addition, the sceptical approach to AI adoption in these newsrooms is rooted in a lack of technical proficiency with AI tools and financial limitations occasioned by the decline in philanthropic funding.

articles.title: The Promise and Practice of Sharing Qualitative Data in Communication Research: Insights from the Qualitative Data Repository
articles.abstract: As open science ideas gain traction in communication and media studies, qualitative researchers face unique challenges and opportunities in adopting transparent and reproducible practices. This article contributes to the growing conversation on open research infrastructures by introducing the Qualitative Data Repository (QDR) as a domain-specific solution for qualitative and multi-method data sharing. QDR is particularly well-equipped to manage data derived from human participants or existing media materials, both of which are widely used in this field. We explore how QDR’s infrastructure, services, and ethical frameworks can be adapted to the needs of communication scholars. First, we briefly outline the benefits of qualitative data sharing—including increased transparency, methodological rigor, and pedagogical value—while acknowledging possible barriers such as ethical concerns, time constraints, and disciplinary histories. We then review practical developments that have taken place over the last five years by scholars practicing some of the principles for trustworthy qualitative communication research laid out by Humphreys et al. (2021). Using examples from a wide variety of projects where QDR has already facilitated data publication and annotations for transparent inquiry, we illustrate how similar practices can be adopted systematically in communication research. We also highlight QDR’s support for researchers throughout the data lifecycle, from planning and consent to curation and controlled access. This article aims to demystify qualitative data sharing and encourage broader adoption among communication and media studies scholars by showcasing QDR’s model and its alignment with findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable principles. We argue that embracing more open and transparent research practices not only enhances the quality and visibility of individual projects but also fosters a more inclusive and collaborative scholarly community.

articles.title: Navigating Online Visibility: Construction of Feminine Identity in Chinese Influencers’ Affective Networked Publics
articles.abstract: The rise of fashion and beauty influencers in China has produced highly visible representations of idealised femininity that increasingly appeal to young women and girls. This study examines how influencers on the Chinese social media platform Weibo discursively construct feminine identity through digital self-branding and how young women interpret and negotiate this mediated feminine visibility. By employing in-depth interviews with 31 Chinese urban young women and a feminist critical discourse analysis of 48 selected posts produced by leading female influencers, this study identifies three interrelated discursive resources through which idealised femininity is assembled: ambiguous feminism, an entrepreneurial beauty discourse, and aspirational consumption. Drawing on Berlant’s concept of intimate publics, the study argues that these discourses circulate affectively through relatability, producing both belonging and discipline within the community. Participants actively negotiate these representations through tactically extracting symbolic values and managing pressures to construct a legible feminine subjectivity. Furthermore, this study argues that asymmetric gendered power relations are reproduced through affective circulation within feminised digital spaces.

articles.title: FOMO in Sub-Saharan African AI Hype: The Quest for a Decolonized AI Adoption Framework
articles.abstract: Based on an abductive analysis of 54 opinion, editorial, and analytical articles published between 2019 and 2025 in nine English-speaking Sub-Saharan African countries, this study examines negotiation of the place of AI within journalism. Conceptualizing AI hype as a form of metajournalistic discourse, the study finds that discussions about AI in journalism in Sub-Saharan Africa are driven by a fear of missing out and a call for a decolonial approach to the technology’s adoption in a way sensitive to the region’s context.
